title: How big is Jupiter's Great Red Spot?

hook.banner: How big is Jupiter's Great Red Spot?

narration.heading: Biggest storm
narration.text: You think hurricanes on Earth are big? This storm could swallow our whole planet.

narration.heading: Jupiter
narration.text: Jupiter is about eleven times wider than Earth. A thousand Earths could fit inside.

narration.heading: Short days
narration.text: And it spins in under ten hours, the shortest day of any planet.

narration.heading: Belts and zones
narration.text: Those stripes are belts and zones, with winds racing east and west in opposite directions.

narration.heading: Great Red Spot
narration.text: Now look south. The Great Red Spot, a storm about one point three times wider than Earth.

narration.heading: Fierce winds
narration.text: Its winds hit nearly five hundred kilometres an hour, and people have watched it since 1831.

narration.heading: Deep roots
narration.text: It reaches hundreds of kilometres down, maybe five hundred, below the cloud tops.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? It's shrinking. About a century ago, three Earths could have fit across it.

narration.heading: Round by 2040
narration.text: At this rate, it could be round by 2040. Do you think it will ever vanish?

skit.text: A storm bigger than Earth, shrinking? Relatable. My storage does that too.

titles: What if a storm could swallow the Earth?
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is shrinking
youtube.description: A spin around Jupiter to the Great Red Spot, a storm wider than Earth that has been watched since 1831, and why it is slowly shrinking.

sources.claim: Jupiter's radius is 69,911 km, about 11 times Earth's width; about 1,000 Earths would fit inside; its day is about 9.9 hours, the shortest in the Solar System; its belts and zones flow east and west in opposite directions

The Great Red Spot sits about 22° S, has winds up to 496 km/h and has been observed since 1831; in 2017 it was 16,350 km wide, about 1.3 times Earth's diameter; it extends roughly 200–500 km below the clouds
The Great Red Spot was largest about a century before 2004, at about 40,000 km, about three times Earth's diameter; at the present rate it would become circular by 2040
